stages.title: Language sounds and pronunciation
stages.hook: Say "cat" and "cut". Do they sound the same? Listen with your ears and your mouth.
explain: English has many sounds. Some words look almost the same but sound different. Cat and cut have different middle sounds.
A word is made of small sounds. We can clap the beats in a word. Banana has three beats: ba-na-na. The loud beat is called the stress.
stages.mnemonic: Clap it out: ba-NA-na. Big clap in the middle!
items: the star in the day sky

gq.q: How many beats (syllables) are in the word "banana"?

gq.why: Rhymes end with the same sound. Cat and hat both end in -at.

panel.q: Why do cat and cut sound different even though only one letter changes?
o: The vowel letter stands for a different sound
English words have no fixed sounds
panel.why: Changing a vowel letter changes the vowel sound, so the word changes.

panel.q: Why is it useful to clap the beats in a new word?
panel.model: Clapping shows how many parts the word has and which one is strong, so you can say it more clearly.
panel.why: Breaking a word into beats helps you say it with the right rhythm.

panel.q: Which word has its loud beat on the first part?
panel.why: We say TA-ble with the strong beat first. The others have the strong beat second.

teach.topic: How to say a word by clapping its beats
teach.model: A word is made of small sounds called beats. You can clap each beat. For example, banana has three claps. One clap is louder than the others.

points.ask: What is a beat in a word?
Which beat is the loudest?
Can you show me one word?

stages.title: Alphabet, script or basic characters
stages.hook: There are 26 letters in English, but more than 40 sounds. How can that be?
explain: English uses the Latin alphabet with 26 letters. Five letters are vowels: a, e, i, o, u. The others are consonants.
Each letter has a name and a sound. The letter B is called "bee" and makes the sound /b/. We write capital letters like A and small letters like a.
stages.mnemonic: A is for apple, B is for ball, C is for cat. Sing the ABC song!
items: a letter that is not a vowel

gq.q: How many letters are in the English alphabet?

gq.why: The vowels are a, e, i, o, u.

panel.q: Why does English need more sounds than letters?
o: Letters can stand for several sounds and some sounds use two letters
Each letter makes exactly one sound
panel.why: English has about 44 sounds. Spellings like sh and th and vowel letters with several sounds make up the difference.

panel.q: The letter Z has two names. What are they and where are they used?
panel.model: Zed is used in British English and zee in American English.
panel.why: Varieties of English name the last letter differently.

panel.q: In which word does the letter "c" make the same sound as "s"?
panel.why: Before e, i or y the letter c often says /s/, as in city.

teach.model: The alphabet is a set of 26 letters. Five are vowels: a, e, i, o, u. The rest are consonants. Each letter has a capital and a small shape.

points.ask: How many letters are there?
Which letters are vowels?
Do letters have different shapes?

stages.title: Greetings and introductions
stages.hook: What do you say when you meet someone for the first time?
explain: We say hello to be friendly. In the morning we can say good morning. At night, before bed, we say good night.
To tell your name, say "My name is" and then your name. To ask someone, say "What is your name?"
stages.mnemonic: Hello, hello, my name is you!
items: a friendly word when we meet
a polite word for a gift
a polite word when you ask
said when you meet someone new

gq.q: Which greeting do you say when you leave?
gq.why: Goodbye is used when we leave.

gq.q: You get a present. What do you say?
gq.why: We say thank you to show we are grateful.

panel.q: Which is more polite when asking for water?
o: Can I have some water, please?
panel.why: Please and a question form are polite.

panel.q: Which greeting is used at about 3 in the afternoon?
panel.why: Good afternoon is for the time after midday until early evening.

panel.q: Why do we say "please" and "thank you"?
panel.model: They are polite words that show respect and kindness to other people.
panel.why: Polite words show manners.

teach.topic: How to greet someone and say your name
teach.model: To greet someone, say hello. Then say "My name is" and your name. You can ask "What is your name?" End with "Nice to meet you."

points.ask: How do I start?
How do I say who I am?
What do I say at the end?

stages.title: Numbers and counting
stages.hook: Can you count from one to ten in English with your fingers?
explain: The numbers from one to ten are one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten. We use them every day to count things.
Numbers can also tell the order. First, second and third show the order. We write 1st, 2nd and 3rd.
stages.mnemonic: One, two, buckle my shoe. Three, four, shut the door.

gq.q: Which word shows order, not amount?
gq.why: Third tells the place in a list.

panel.q: How do you say 2 + 3 = 5 aloud?
o: Two and three are five times
panel.why: We say plus and equals.

panel.q: Which number word has the loud beat on the first part?
panel.why: We say THIR-ty, but thir-TEEN. The -teen numbers are stressed at the end, which helps tell them from the -ty numbers.

panel.q: Why do we say "one apple" but "two apples"?
panel.model: English adds -s to a noun when there is more than one.
panel.why: Plural nouns usually take -s.

teach.model: Say the numbers in order: one, two, three and so on to ten. You can count fingers or toys. After ten comes eleven.

points.ask: What do I say first?
Where do I stop?
What can I count?

stages.title: Colours and shapes
stages.hook: The sky is blue and grass is green. What colour is a banana?
explain: Colours have names in English: red, blue, yellow, green, orange, purple, black and white.
Shapes have names too. A circle is round. A square has four equal sides. A triangle has three sides.
stages.mnemonic: Red like a rose, blue like the sea, yellow like the sun, green like a tree.

gq.q: Where does the colour word go in English?
o: Before the noun: a red ball
After the noun: a ball red
At the start of the sentence
gq.why: English puts the colour before the noun.

gq.q: How many sides does a triangle have?

panel.q: Which is correct?
panel.why: Size usually comes before colour in English.

panel.q: Why do we say "a red apple" but "an orange"?
panel.model: We use an before a word that starts with a vowel sound, like orange.
panel.why: A becomes an before a vowel sound.

panel.q: Which word is the American spelling of the British "colour"?
panel.why: American English spells it color.

teach.model: Colours are words like red and blue. They go before a noun, as in a red ball. Shapes are circle, square and triangle.

points.ask: Can you say a colour?
Where does the colour word go?
What is a shape?

stages.title: Family and people
stages.hook: Who lives in your home? What do you call each person?
explain: A family has people with special names. There are a mother and a father. A child can be a son or a daughter. They can have a brother or a sister.
The words grandmother and grandfather are for the parents of your parents. People often say mum or mom, and dad.
stages.mnemonic: Mum and Dad, Gran and Grandpa, brother and sister: my family tree!
items: a boy in the family, child of the parents
a girl in the family, child of the parents
a person who is your friend

gq.q: Which word means your father's brother?
gq.why: An uncle is the brother of a parent.

gq.q: Which spelling of "mum" is used in American English?
gq.why: Americans say mom; British speakers say mum.

panel.q: Which sentence is correct?
panel.why: We use is with she.

panel.q: What is the difference between "my" and "mine"?
panel.model: My comes before a noun (my book). Mine stands alone (the book is mine).
panel.why: Possessive adjective versus pronoun.

panel.q: Your mother's mother is your...
panel.why: The mother of your mother is your grandmother.

teach.model: Family words name the people in a family: mother, father, brother and sister. Grandparents are the parents of your parents. We say my before the word, like my sister.

points.ask: Which words name a family?
What do I call my parent's parent?
How do I say this is mine?

stages.title: Common objects
stages.hook: Look around you. How many things can you name in English?
explain: Objects are things we use. A table, a chair, a door and a window are in many homes. A pen and a book are for school.
Use a or an before one thing: a table, an apple. For many things, add -s: two books.
stages.mnemonic: Touch it and say it: table, chair, door, bed.
items: we open it to go in
we carry school things in it
sentences: The book is on the table.

gq.why: Apple starts with a vowel sound, so we say an apple.

panel.q: What is the plural of "box"?
panel.why: Nouns ending in x add -es.

panel.q: Where is the book?  "The book is ___ the table."
panel.why: On means touching the top of a surface.

panel.q: Why do we say "the" in "the book is on the table" but "a" in "I have a book"?
panel.model: The is for a particular thing we both know; a is for any one thing.
panel.why: Definite and indefinite articles.

teach.model: Objects have names. Say a before one thing, like a chair. Add -s for many, like chairs. Say where it is with on or in.

points.ask: What small word goes before one thing?
How do I talk about many?
How do I say where it is?

stages.title: Everyday actions
stages.hook: What can you do with your body? Walk? Jump? Clap?
explain: Verbs are action words. We run, jump, eat, drink, sleep and read. A short sentence with I and a verb tells what you do: I run.
With he or she, a verb often takes -s: she runs, he eats. To say what you are doing now, use am, is or are plus a verb ending in -ing.
stages.mnemonic: I run, he runs, she runs: the S sits down with she, he and it.
items: to take food into your mouth
to make a song with your voice

gq.why: With he, she and it, the present verb takes -s.

gq.q: Which word shows an action happening now?
gq.why: Is plus a verb with -ing shows an action in progress.

panel.q: Choose the correct sentence.
panel.why: They takes are.

panel.q: What is the -ing form of "run"?
panel.why: A short word with one vowel and one final consonant doubles the last letter.

panel.q: What is the difference between "I read" and "I am reading"?
panel.model: I read describes a habit or fact; I am reading is happening now.
panel.why: Simple present versus present continuous.

teach.model: A verb is an action word, like run or eat. With I you use the plain verb. With he or she add -s. For now, say am, is or are plus -ing.

points.ask: What is a verb?
What changes with he or she?
How do I say it is happening now?

stages.title: Simple listening and speaking
stages.hook: Listen to a friend say "Hello, how are you?" What do you say back?
explain: When we talk, we listen first and then answer. A common question is "How are you?" We can answer "I am fine, thank you."
If you do not hear well, say "Sorry?" or "Can you say that again, please?" That is a good way to learn.
stages.mnemonic: Ears first, mouth second. Listen, then say.

gq.q: Someone says "Thank you." What is a polite answer?
You did not hear the teacher. What can you say?
o: Can you say that again, please?
gq.why: It is a polite request to repeat.

panel.q: "How are you?" in a shop is usually...
o: a polite greeting, not a long medical question
panel.why: In many English-speaking places it is a friendly greeting and a short answer is expected.

panel.q: Why is it good to listen before you answer?
panel.model: Listening helps you understand the question so that you can give a correct answer.
panel.why: Understanding comes first.

panel.q: Which word has the loud beat on the second part?
panel.why: We say hel-LO, with the stress on the second part.

teach.topic: Listening and answering in a talk
teach.model: Listen first, then answer. If a person says How are you? you can say I am fine, thank you. If you do not understand, ask them to say it again slowly.

points.ask: What do I do first?
What can I say to How are you?
What if I do not understand?
